segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He entered Jericho and was passing through.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a man there named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, for he was short in stature.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree to see him, because Jesus was about to pass that way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came to the place, Jesus looked up and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he hurried down and welcomed him with joy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they saw it, they all began to grumble, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has gone in to be the guest of a sinful man.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I pay back four times as much.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were listening to this, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man of noble birth traveled to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He called ten of his slaves, gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Do business with this until I come back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But his fellow citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered the slaves to whom he had given the money to be called to him, so that he might learn what they had gained by doing business.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The first came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has earned ten minas more.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you are to have authority over ten cities.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The second came and said, ‘Your mina, master, has made five minas.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to this one too, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the other came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down and reap what you did not sow.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked slave! You knew, did you, that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then why did you not put my money in the bank? Then when I came I would have collected it with interest.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And to those standing by he said, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They said to him, ‘Master, he has ten minas!’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After saying this, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came near Bethphage and Bethany, at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the village opposite, and as you enter it you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord needs it.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who were sent went off and found it just as he had told them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why are you untying the colt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Lord needs it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he went along, they kept spreading their cloaks on the road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was now drawing near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the deeds of power they had seen,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I tell you, if these are silent, the stones will cry out.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If only you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace—but now they have been hidden from your eyes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a palisade against you and surround you and hem you in on every side,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they will dash you to the ground, you and your children within you, and will not leave one stone upon another within you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it ‘a den of bandits.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy him, as were the leading men of the people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but they could not find anything they could do, for all the people hung on his words as they listened.

notes.note: The Greek verbs “give” and “pay back” are in the present tense. Most interpreters take them as a resolve made on the spot (“I am now giving”), which fits Jesus’ reply that salvation has come “today.” A minority reads them as Zacchaeus’s existing practice, offered in his own defense against the crowd’s grumbling. The plain English present leaves both readings open.

The verb means to squeeze money out of someone by false charges or intimidation, which “defrauded” or “cheated” understates. It is the same verb used in Luke 3:14, where soldiers are told not to do this. Fourfold repayment echoes the heaviest restitution the Law of Moses prescribes for theft.

Here the word means royal authority, the right to rule as king, not a territory: the nobleman travels to a higher power to be confirmed as king over his own country. Hearers would probably have recalled Archelaus, son of Herod the Great, who went to Rome to have his rule confirmed while a delegation of his subjects went to oppose him, as Josephus reports. “Kingdom” is kept so that the link with “the kingdom of God” in verse 11 stays audible.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and standard lexicons gloss it as “slave.” Most English versions soften it to “servant.” In the ancient world slaves were often entrusted with managing money and business, as here.

A mina was a sum of one hundred drachmas, roughly three to four months’ wages for a day laborer. Each slave receives one mina. It is a far smaller sum than the talent in the similar parable in Matthew 25, which is why the king calls it “a very small matter.”

The Greek does not mark who speaks this sentence. It is rendered here as the king’s reply to the bystanders’ objection, since verse 27 continues in the king’s voice. It can also be read as Jesus stepping outside the story to state its point to his own hearers; the same saying appears on Jesus’ lips in Luke 8:18.

notes.traditional: The Lord has need of it
notes.note: The Greek can also be construed as “Its master needs it,” with “its” attached to “Lord” rather than to “needs.” The same word, in the plural, is used for the colt’s “owners” in verse 33, so the reply sets one claim of ownership against another. Most translations render as here.

The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used here of concrete acts that display it. “Deeds of power” keeps that connection visible; “miracles” and “mighty works” are equally acceptable renderings, and there is no dispute about the meaning.

notes.phrase: Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord
notes.note: The disciples adapt Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the festivals: “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.” Luke’s wording adds “the king,” making the royal claim explicit. The second line recalls the angels’ song at Jesus’ birth in Luke 2:14.

In the Greek Scriptures a “visitation” is God’s coming to look upon his people, whether to rescue or to judge. Here it is the gracious kind: God has come to Jerusalem in Jesus, and the city has not recognized it. Luke uses the related verb in the same sense in 1:68 and 7:16, “God has visited his people.”

The Greek word denotes a violent, often armed plunderer such as a highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. Most modern versions use “robbers,” which is not wrong; “bandits” keeps the note of violence and outlawry. Jesus joins Isaiah 56:7 to Jeremiah 7:11, where the “den” is the hideout in which bandits feel safe after their crimes.
